1:
The fire falls when the praying ends, and Henry fixes on the timing: it came down not upon the killing of the sacrifices but upon the praying of the prayer, as it had for Moses and Gideon and David and Elijah, since to accept a burnt-sacrifice is in the Hebrew phrase to turn it to ashes. He finds the sign double. It shows God glorious in himself, a consuming fire breaking out, as it is probable, from the thick darkness, so that the sinners in Sion had reason to ask who shall dwell near this devouring fire; and gracious to Israel, since the fire which might justly have consumed them fastened instead on the sacrifice offered in their stead. Clarke sets it in sequence: the cloud had come down before, and now the fire consumes the offering, showing that both the house and the sacrifices were accepted. Ellicott compares the fire at the consecration in Leviticus and thinks it likely this one descended after Solomon had blessed the people. Wesley keeps to the token and draws the application Henry draws too, that the surest evidence of God's acceptance of our prayers is the descent of his holy fire upon us.

Whether the chronicler invented any of it is the modern question, and two voices meet it. Ellicott marks this verse as the point where the two accounts diverge and then defends the writer: there is no objective ground for supposing he invented the facts, he must have found them in one of his sources, and it is gratuitous to fancy him more partial to miracle than the older historian, his greater interest in everything concerning the worship of the temple being enough to account for this and similar additions. Delitzsch reports the charge itself, that because the narrative is absent from Kings, where a speech of Solomon to the congregation stands instead, modern criticism has rejected it as a later unhistorical embellishment of the dedication.

The glory is treated as a separate thing from the fire. Ellicott insists the statement is no mere duplicate of the earlier chapter, that the glory is apparently a manifestation quite distinct from the fire, and that the writer plainly means to record two distinct appearances of it, one before and one after the prayer of consecration, each attended by the same effect on the ministering priests. Gill wonders whether a distinct fire is meant as well, since this one seems to come down upon the house and may denote a bright shining light; and he explains the priests' difficulty, that they had gone in to carry the ark and, unable to stand and minister, came out and could not re-enter. Wesley orders it differently again: the cloud came down upon the house first and then entered it, so that it was seen within by the priests and without by the people.

The people answer from the pavement. Ellicott glosses the word, rendered in the Greek by the term that reappears in John and compared with a tesselated floor, notes an infinitive standing for the finite verb, and reports a Syriac and Arabic paraphrase in which the people say to one another, Give thanks to the Lord; that last phrase, he adds, is almost the only thing in the section which can be called characteristic of the chronicler's own style. Wesley reads the posture as three things at once, their awful dread of the divine majesty, their cheerful submission to his authority, and their sense of utter unworthiness to come into his presence. Delitzsch simply records that the congregation, seeing the fire and the glory descend, bowed with their faces to the ground and worshipped.
4:
Who actually killed the victims is left open, and Clarke offers both answers: either the people presented them to the priests, who slew them and sprinkled the blood, or the people slew them themselves and, having caught the blood and collected the fat, presented those to the priests to be offered as the law required. Ellicott keeps to the Hebrew, where the verse opens with a plain and rather than a then and the people are simply sacrificing a sacrifice. On the great total Clarke explains that the twenty-two thousand oxen are the sum of all the victims offered through both weeks, the seven days of the feast and the seven of the dedication; Ellicott notes the numbers agree exactly with the older account, which adds that these were peace offerings, words that seem to have dropped out here, and which keeps the older forms, sons of Israel and house of Jehovah where this text has the people and the house of God. Delitzsch says only that the dedication was concluded by a great thank-offering, and that the account of it agrees completely with Kings.

The sixth verse is the chronicler's own, and Ellicott says why: it is added after his usual fashion of laying stress on the ritual, and especially on its choral and musical side. He renders the priests as standing at their posts upon their watches, takes the instruments of music of the Lord to mean sacred music as we should say, and corrects the Greek on the closing phrase, which treats the word substantively as though it meant in David's psalmody, perhaps with the great hallel of the synagogue in view; the English gives the true sense, that the Levites were David's ministers of praise. Gill divides the work, some of the priests offering sacrifices and others blowing trumpets. Wesley explains the arrangement from its origin, that David composed the psalms, appointed the Levites to sing them, and joined instrumental music to their voices.

The last verse explains an awkwardness in the older text. Ellicott notes that it is slightly modified from Kings, and that where Kings says the brazen altar was too little to receive the offerings this writer explains rather that it was not able to receive them, both offerings standing in the singular in the Hebrew. Delitzsch treats the whole verse as a supplementary remark whose connective expresses only the sequence of thought, so that its verb should be read as a pluperfect. Gill, noting that the dedication of the altar is mentioned here as though distinct from the dedication of the house and the hallowing of the middle of the court, turns aside to the pagans who imitated the practice, dedicating their altars with ashes and water as Pausanias relates and holding feasts at the dedication of their temples; in which, he adds, they have themselves been imitated by Christians, many of our country feasts having first been kept at the dedication of a church to one saint or another.
8:
The feast is dated and bounded. Ellicott identifies it as Tabernacles, kept for its legal seven days counted from the fifteenth of the seventh month, and reads the southern limit as a torrent or wady rather than a river; the older account, he notes, adds that it was kept before the Lord our God. Clarke takes the northern limit from the Targum, which stretches it from the entrance of Antioch to the Nile of Egypt. Delitzsch marks the whole passage as the close of the dedication proper.

Then comes the arithmetic that has puzzled readers of the older book. Ellicott makes the eighth day the twenty-second of the month and observes that the solemn assembly held on it is not mentioned in Kings at all, which says only that on the eighth day Solomon dismissed the people. His solution to the harder problem is historical rather than textual: the week before Tabernacles began, the eighth to the fourteenth of Ethanim or Tisri, had been kept as an extraordinary festival for the inauguration of the house, and Tabernacles then ran its own course afterwards, which is what the obscure phrase in Kings about seven days and seven days, fourteen days, is compressing into one clause. The Syriac, he adds, spells the same thing out, seven days of the feast and seven days of the inauguration of the house, these and these amounting to fourteen.

The day of dismissal is harmonised two different ways. Ellicott simply observes that the twenty-third begins with the evening of the twenty-second, so that no real discrepancy exists, and notes that some copies and the eastern versions insert all before the goodness, as the older text does. Clarke reaches the same peace by a different road, reporting Jarchi: the king gave the people liberty to return on the eighth day and many did then return, and he dismissed the remainder on the ninth, which is the twenty-third once the fourteen days of the two feasts are reckoned in. Clarke also passes on the Targum's expansion of the verse, where the people go home glad for the good done to David, on whose account the doors of the sanctuary stood open, and for Solomon, because his prayer was heard and the majesty of the Lord had rested on the house, and for Israel, because their oblations were favourably accepted and the heavenly fire had come down and devoured their sacrifices.

Two small additions close the section. Ellicott notes that where Kings has David his servant, this writer adds the mention of Solomon, consistently with his habit of connecting all Solomon's success with the promise made to David; and that the last verse paraphrases all the desire of Solomon which he willed to do, its remainder being wanting in Kings altogether. Gill observes only that from this point the narrative runs with the older account.
12:
God answers twice over, and Henry separates the two answers carefully. The fire had already shown that the prayer was accepted, but a prayer may be accepted and yet not answered in the letter of it, so God appears by night as he had once before, and after a day of sacrifice as then, to give a particular reply. What he grants, on Henry's reading, is that the house shall be owned as a house of sacrifice for Israel and a house of prayer for all people, the promise that his name shall be there for ever meaning that there he will make himself known and there he will be called upon. Clarke notes it was a second manifestation and passes on the Targum, where it is the Word of the Lord that appears. Ellicott observes that the night is only implied in the older text, which says instead that he appeared as he had at Gibeon, and that the phrase house of sacrifice occurs nowhere else in the Old Testament.

Where the addition came from Ellicott and Delitzsch both consider. Ellicott marks this verse as the start of what the chronicler adds to the prayer as the older text has it, and argues from the style that the added section must have formed an integral part of an original narrative from which both writers drew, rather than being composed later. Delitzsch grants that the general contents and the order of the thoughts agree in the two accounts and locates the differences in the individual expressions. Gill makes the same point from the content: everything from here to the end runs with the older book except the verses answering Solomon's particular requests about famine and pestilence, which are given as a specimen and as encouragement to expect the same treatment in every other case he had named.

The conditions are then set out, and the two schools read them differently. Ellicott works each clause to its parallel, taking called by my name to mean dedicated to me, and tracing the humbling, the seeking of the face, the turning from wicked ways and the healing of the land each to its own passage elsewhere; the locust here, he notes, is a winged and edible species, where the chapter before had named two other kinds. Clarke adds only the Targum's gloss, that the pestilence is the angel of death, and its rendering of the opened eyes, that it shall be pleasing in the sight of the Word to incline his ear. Henry reads the sequence as a national doctrine. Judgments are supposed, and by the locusts devouring the land he thinks enemies may be meant, as greedy as locusts and laying all waste. Repentance is then required, and he puts the demand sharply: God expects that a people who have dishonoured his name by their iniquity should honour it by accepting the punishment of their iniquity. They must humble themselves under his hand, pray for the judgment's removal and seek his face, and yet all this will not do unless they turn from their wicked ways and return to the God from whom they have revolted. Only then is mercy promised, that he will forgive the sin which brought the judgment and heal the land by redressing every grievance. With the choosing and sanctifying of the house at the close, Ellicott notes, the two accounts run parallel again, the perpetually of the English standing for a plainer all the days.
17:
Only two witnesses work this closing section, and they divide the labour between text and event. Ellicott takes the condition offered Solomon back to its wording: the older book adds that he must walk in perfectness of heart and in uprightness, and where this text runs and to do, Kings has an infinitive defining the verb before it. On the covenant he notes that the Hebrew says only I cut for David, the word covenant being left out, so the Syriac renders it I sware; Kings has I spake concerning David, and the verb for cutting may be an ancient misreading of the verb for speaking, the two being much alike in Hebrew writing. And where Kings promises a successor from upon the throne of Israel, this text promises a ruler in Israel, a phrase Ellicott thinks borrowed from Micah to repair a defective text in which the word throne had dropped out. Clarke answers the whole promise in a sentence: it was not fulfilled because the condition was not fulfilled, for they forsook God, and he cut them off, and the throne with them.

The threat that follows has been softened, and Ellicott shows where. The order of the words implies that and your children has fallen out here, as the older book and the eastern versions both have it; Kings emphasises the verb, if turn ye will, adds from after me, and says keep not where this says forsake. The plucking up by the roots therefore has those children for its object, the opposite thought being that of planting a nation in a land; and twice over the harsher phrase of Kings is eased, for where that book would cut off Israel from the face of the land and let Israel become a byword, this one plucks up and makes it so. The exact phrase for casting out of sight, Ellicott adds, occurs nowhere else. Clarke reads the same verse as a record rather than a warning: how completely it has been fulfilled, since not only have the branches of the Jewish political tree been cut off but the very roots plucked up, so that the day of the Lord's anger has left them neither root nor branch.

The house that is high is probably a house in ruins. Ellicott calls the English a correction of the older reading, that this house shall be high, which appears meaningless where it stands; but the Syriac and Arabic in both books read that it shall be laid waste, and the Targum of Kings combines the two, so the original was most likely that this house shall become ruinous heaps, the Hebrew for heaps and for high differing very little. The mistake, he observes, is as old as the Greek. He reverses the next clause too, which should say that everyone passing by shall be astonished, notes that the Syriac has the passer-by shake his head and sway with his hand before he speaks, and judges the hiss that Kings adds to be certainly original.

What the passer-by says closes the book. Ellicott renders it simply that men shall say, and notes that where this text has he brought the older one names Jehovah. Clarke supplies the reason, and does it as a general law: while they cleaved to God the most powerful enemy could make no impression on them, but once they forsook him the weakest of their foes harassed and oppressed them and reduced them to bondage. It was by no personal prowess, he insists, no genuine heroism and no supereminent military tactics that the Jews overcame their enemies, but by the divine power alone, destitute of which they were even worse than other men; and he ends on the symmetry, that no nation was ever so highly favoured and none ever so severely and signally punished.
